name: Trachea
func: The windpipe: a stiff but flexible tube that carries air from the larynx down to the lungs. C-shaped cartilage rings keep it open, and its sticky, hair-lined lining traps dust and sweeps it back up.

levels.kid:
The **trachea** is your windpipe. It's a tube in the front of your neck that carries air down into your chest, where it splits into two tubes, one for each lung.

If you gently touch the front of your neck below your voice box, you can feel bumpy rings. Those are rings of **cartilage**, the same bendy stuff that's in your ears. They're shaped like the letter C and they keep the windpipe open, like the rings inside a vacuum cleaner hose, so it never squashes flat.

The inside is lined with sticky goo and tiny hairs called **cilia**. When you breathe in dust or germs, they get stuck in the goo, and the little hairs sweep it all up toward your throat so you can cough it out or swallow it.
levels.hs:
The **trachea** runs from the bottom of the **larynx** (at the **cricoid cartilage**, about the level of **C6**) down to about the level of the **sternal angle (T4/T5)**, where it divides into the right and left **main bronchi**. In adults it is about **10–12 cm long** and about 2 cm wide.

It lies in the midline, in front of the **esophagus**. In the neck, the **isthmus of the thyroid gland** crosses in front of its 2nd–4th rings, and the thyroid lobes hug its sides. In the chest it passes through the superior mediastinum with the **brachiocephalic artery** and the **arch of the aorta** curving in front and to the left.

Its wall has **16–20 C-shaped rings of hyaline cartilage**. The gap at the back of each "C" is closed by the **trachealis muscle**, a band of smooth muscle. This design keeps the airway open but lets the esophagus behind it bulge forward when you swallow a big bite of food.

The lining is **respiratory epithelium**: tall cells with **cilia** plus **goblet cells** that make mucus. Together they form the **mucociliary escalator**, which carries trapped particles upward at a few millimetres per minute.
levels.college:
The trachea's wall has four layers: **mucosa** (pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium with goblet cells on a lamina propria rich in elastic fibres), **submucosa** with seromucous glands, the **hyaline cartilage** layer, and an outer **adventitia**.

The last ring at the bottom is shaped into a keel-like ridge, the **carina**, at the bifurcation. The carina's mucosa is one of the most cough-sensitive spots in the airway.

**Blood supply**: the cervical trachea is fed mainly by the **inferior thyroid arteries**, the thoracic trachea by the **bronchial arteries**. Small vessels enter from the sides in segments, so the trachea can be devascularised if it is stripped too far around, which matters in surgery.

**Nerves**: the **recurrent laryngeal nerves** run up in the **tracheoesophageal grooves** on each side, giving sensory and secretomotor branches to the trachea before entering the larynx. Parasympathetic fibres come from the vagus and sympathetic fibres from the sympathetic trunks.

**Lymph** drains to the pretracheal, paratracheal and tracheobronchial nodes.

The trachea is also mobile: it lengthens and shortens with breathing and neck movement, and the carina moves down a few centimetres on deep inspiration. In the supine position, the bifurcation sits roughly at T4/T5, but in standing deep inspiration it may descend to T6.

The anatomy explains a practical point: the **right main bronchus** is wider, shorter and more vertical, so inhaled objects and a too-deep breathing tube usually go right.
levels.phd:
The respiratory epithelium contains several cell types. **Ciliated cells** each carry about 200–300 motile cilia with the classic **9+2 axoneme**; **dynein arms** generate a coordinated wave (metachronal rhythm) beating at around 10–15 Hz. **Goblet cells** secrete **mucins** (mainly MUC5AC and MUC5B). **Basal cells** are the stem cells that regenerate the epithelium. There are also **club cells**, rare **neuroendocrine cells**, chemosensory **tuft (brush) cells**, and the CFTR-rich **ionocytes** discovered by single-cell sequencing in 2018.

Effective clearance needs two layers: a watery **periciliary layer** in which cilia beat, and a gel-like mucus layer on top. The height of the periciliary layer is set by ion transport: **CFTR** secretes chloride and bicarbonate, while **ENaC** absorbs sodium. In **cystic fibrosis**, defective CFTR dehydrates the surface, mucus becomes thick, clearance fails and chronic infection follows.

**Primary ciliary dyskinesia** (mutations in dynein-arm genes such as DNAH5) stops cilia from beating effectively, causing chronic sinus and lung infection; about half of patients have **situs inversus** (Kartagener syndrome), because motile cilia in the embryonic node set left–right asymmetry.

Developmentally, the trachea forms from the **laryngotracheal (respiratory) diverticulum**, budding from the ventral foregut around week 4. The **tracheoesophageal septum** separates it from the esophagus; failure produces **tracheoesophageal fistula** with **esophageal atresia**.

Cough is triggered by **vagal afferents** (rapidly adapting receptors and C fibres, many expressing TRPV1 and TRPA1) relaying to the **nucleus tractus solitarius** in the medulla. Tissue engineering of tracheal replacements remains an unsolved research problem; several early synthetic transplants failed badly.
levels.expert:
**Exam**: the trachea should be **midline** in the suprasternal notch. **Tracheal deviation** away from the affected side suggests tension pneumothorax or a large effusion; toward it suggests lung collapse or pneumonectomy. A large goitre can push it aside or narrow it. **Stridor** (a high-pitched noisy breath, mainly on inspiration for upper airway problems) means narrowing and is a warning sign.

**Imaging**: chest X-ray shows the tracheal air column and the carinal angle (widened by an enlarged left atrium or subcarinal lymph nodes). **CT** with 3D reconstruction and **bronchoscopy** assess stenosis, tumours and foreign bodies.

**Airway procedures**:
- **Endotracheal intubation**: the tube tip should sit a few centimetres above the carina; too deep and it usually enters the right main bronchus, ventilating only one lung.
- **Emergency cricothyrotomy**: an opening through the **cricothyroid membrane**, between thyroid and cricoid cartilages, when intubation fails ("can't intubate, can't oxygenate").
- **Tracheostomy**: usually through the 2nd–4th rings, with care for the thyroid isthmus, anterior jugular veins and, low in the neck, the brachiocephalic artery. A late feared complication is **tracheo-innominate artery fistula**, often preceded by a small "herald bleed".

**Post-intubation tracheal stenosis** results from cuff pressure causing mucosal ischaemia. **Tracheomalacia** (soft, collapsing walls) occurs in children and after long compression.

**Neurosurgical relevance**: **anterior cervical spine surgery** (ACDF) retracts the trachea and esophagus to reach the vertebral bodies, and stretching can injure the **recurrent laryngeal nerve** in the tracheoesophageal groove, causing hoarseness. Prolonged-ventilation patients in neuro-ICU often need tracheostomy.

keyPoints: Runs from cricoid (C6) to carina (about T4/T5)
16–20 C-shaped cartilage rings, open at the back (trachealis)
Mucociliary escalator clears dust and germs
Right main bronchus is wider and more vertical
Midline position is a key exam sign

test.q: Where does the trachea divide into the main bronchi?
test.explain: The bifurcation sits at roughly the sternal angle, about T4/T5, in a supine person.

test.q: The smooth muscle that closes the back of each tracheal ring is the ______.
test.explain: The trachealis spans the open back of each C-shaped ring, next to the esophagus.

test.q: Why do inhaled peanuts usually end up in the right lung?
choices: The right bronchus is wider and more vertical
The left bronchus has no cartilage
test.explain: The right main bronchus is shorter, wider and more in line with the trachea.

test.q: A patient's trachea is pushed away from the side of absent breath sounds, with low blood pressure. Most likely?
test.explain: Tension pneumothorax shifts the mediastinum and trachea away from the affected side and is an emergency.

test.q: Defective ciliary beating plus situs inversus is called ______ syndrome.
test.explain: Kartagener syndrome is the subset of primary ciliary dyskinesia with situs inversus.
